ECE 6390 / Exam 2

Read This Guide as One Satellite Link

Fig. 1 shows where each chapter acts on the same physical link. A geostationary satellite radiates a beam toward a ground station; the ground station turns the arriving field back into bits; a separate set of navigation satellites lets a handheld receiver measure where it is. Each chapter answers one question about that picture, and each answer becomes the input to the next chapter.

One running example threads through the guide. A geostationary satellite at Atlanta’s longitude sends a 10 GHz downlink to a 1 m dish in Atlanta. Chapter II gives the dish’s gain, Chapter IV its look angle, slant range and received power, and Chapter VII its noise, symbol-energy ratio and decision quality. Following one set of numbers from antenna to decision shows exactly where each formula’s inputs come from.

Table I collects the running example’s independent choices. Geometry, frequency, antenna efficiency, transmitter settings and receiver assumptions enter at different points; the later chapters calculate their consequences. The model assumes far-field free-space propagation, matched pointing and polarization, and no extra feeder, rain or implementation losses. Those choices isolate the course calculations rather than predict a complete operating satellite link. The symbol rate, received quality ratios and noisy decisions are derived or simulated later; they are not additional measured givens.

Practice

1. Double the range while keeping frequency, power, gains and excess losses fixed. How do received power and free-space path loss change?

Use the inverse-square range dependence and 20 log10 of the range ratio.

Received power becomes one quarter, about 6.02 dB lower. Free-space path loss increases by about 6.02 dB. Receiver noise is unchanged if its temperature and equivalent bandwidth are unchanged.
